cues.text: A Dream Formed in Girlhood
Born on August 29, 1769, at Grenoble, France, to a wealthy and influential family, Philippine Duchesne was educated at the Visitation convent of Sainte-Marie d'en Haut in her native city.

There, a visiting Jesuit's stories of missionary labor among Native American tribes in Louisiana kindled in her a longing to serve as a missionary herself—a dream that would not find its fulfillment for nearly fifty years.
The upheaval of the French Revolution closed her convent and scattered its community, but Philippine's resolve for religious life survived the disruption intact.
Joining the Society of the Sacred Heart
When St. Madeleine Sophie Barat sought to expand her newly founded Society of the Sacred Heart to Grenoble, Philippine placed her own small remaining community under Barat's direction.
She became a novice in the new congregation and formed a close and lasting friendship with its foundress.

For over a decade Philippine served the Society at home, first in its school at Sainte-Marie and later as secretary general — faithful, demanding administrative work that never entirely displaced her original missionary hope.

Sophie Barat and Philippine remained close correspondents and friends across the following decades, even as duty kept the younger woman's own missionary hope indefinitely deferred, a patience she bore without ever setting the dream aside.
A Call Finally Answered

In 1817, Bishop William Dubourg of Louisiana invited the Society to establish schools for Native American and French children in his vast frontier diocese, and Sophie Barat, recognizing the moment Philippine had waited for, sent her at last.

In March 1818, at forty-eight years old, Philippine sailed from France with four companions, landing near New Orleans on the feast of the Sacred Heart before making her way up the Mississippi to St. Louis.
The Remotest Village in the United States
Rather than the mission among Native Americans she had long hoped for, Philippine and her sisters were directed instead to St. Charles, Missouri .
She described the settlement with disappointed candor as "the remotest village in the United States."
There, on September 14, 1818, they opened the Society of the Sacred Heart's first house outside Europe and the first free school west of the Mississippi River.
They worked in genuine frontier poverty that she called, without bitterness, the true riches of a missionary priest's or sister's life.
The community soon relocated to Florissant, Missouri, where Philippine opened the Society's first American novitiate in 1820.
Even amid this frontier hardship, the young Society of the Sacred Heart, planted first in a single log cabin, took root steadily across Missouri and Louisiana, one small foundation at a time.
A Dream Fulfilled at Seventy-One
Only in 1841, at seventy-one years old, did Philippine finally reach the mission among Native Americans she had dreamed of as a girl.
After more than two decades of school-building on the American frontier, she traveled to Sugar Creek, Kansas, to help establish a school for Potawatomi girls.

Too frail by then for physical labor and unable to master the Potawatomi language, she spent her time there chiefly in silent, constant prayer, so that the Potawatomi themselves gave her the name Quah-kah-ka-num-ad — "Woman Who Prays Always."
Legacy
Recalled to St. Charles after a single year in Kansas, Philippine spent her final decade in prayer and quiet retirement, dying there on November 18, 1852, at eighty-three.
She was beatified by Pope Pius XII in 1940 and canonized by Pope John Paul II on July 3, 1988.
Honored today as patroness of those who must persevere amid long delay and disappointment, Rose Philippine Duchesne remains a companion for every believer.
She speaks especially to those who have carried a single, unwavering desire for decades before finally, however imperfectly and however late, seeing it fulfilled.
